# Forensic Dossier — Dürr AG (DUE.DE)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, covering eight consecutive quarterly calls from May 2024 through the March 2026 preliminary-results call.*

Dürr is a German industrial-machinery group. It builds the giant paint shops and final-assembly lines that car factories run on (its Automotive division), the automation and testing equipment that sits inside factories (Industrial Automation, anchored by the acquired BBS Automation and the Schenck balancing business), and woodworking machinery for the furniture and timber-house industries (its majority-owned, separately-listed HOMAG division). Over the period covered here the company shrank itself on purpose — from five divisions to three — and sold its environmental-technology arm.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management told evolved cleanly and consistently from "grow through acquisition" to "simplify, cut costs, and lift margins." In early 2024 the emphasis was on record order intake (a new quarterly high of EUR 1.5 billion in the first quarter of 2024), a record backlog of EUR 4.6 billion, and the freshly-bought BBS Automation building "the second-largest player in industrial automation." The growth driver introduced most enthusiastically back then — electric-vehicle battery-coating equipment ("we see a lot of potential in the battery business") — was quietly demoted quarter after quarter, and by the end was openly described as a problem: "it's tough to be quite fair at the moment, that's why we are restructuring" (third quarter of 2025). The battery unit was eventually impaired and folded into the Automotive division at the start of 2026.

In its place, three new threads took over the narrative: (1) the portfolio simplification — selling the Agramkow refrigeration-systems unit (mid-2024), then the much larger environmental-technology business (closed October 31, 2025), and collapsing five divisions into three (live January 1, 2025); (2) a "value before volume" pricing discipline that the company credits for steadily rising margins; and (3) cost cutting — first the EUR 50 million HOMAG program, then a further EUR 50 million administrative-savings program (about 500 jobs by end-2026). The arc is coherent: this is a deliberate, multi-year self-help and de-conglomeration story, not a growth story.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Value before volume" is lifting margins | EBIT margin before extraordinaries rose from 4.9% (Q1 2024) to a full-year 5.6% in 2025, above the 4.5–5.5% target corridor; Automotive hit 11% in Q4 2025 | **Matches.** The margin trajectory is real and the single most credible part of the story. |
| Strong, even record, demand | Order intake fell 29% in the first nine months of 2025 and another 11% in Q1 2026; revenue declined from EUR 4.63B (2023) to EUR 4.17B (2025), a roughly 3% drop year-on-year with a slightly negative three-year trend | **Diverges.** The demand narrative is richer than the trajectory justifies — most of the "record" order figures were flattered by one EUR 500M German automotive order in early 2024 that did not repeat. |
| Net profit doubled / soaring earnings | 2025 group net income of EUR 206 million did double — but EUR 227 million of it was the one-time book gain on the environmental-technology sale; continuing operations actually posted a EUR 50 million net loss after a EUR 135 million impairment | **Misleading if taken at face value.** The headline EPS of 2.92 (up 107%) and the "doubled net income" are largely a disposal gain, not operating earnings power. The system's own trailing-twelve-month figures (EPS 2.85, free cash flow EUR 292M) and the latest-quarter EPS down 15% year-on-year are the cleaner read. |
| Free cash flow is strong | 2025 continuing free cash flow of EUR 162 million beat the EUR 0–50 million guide — but the CFO openly warned roughly EUR 100 million was pulled-forward customer prepayments that "is missing as a cash inflow in 2026," and guided 2026 free cash flow back to EUR 0–50 million | **Matches, with an honest asterisk.** Cash generation is genuine but lumpy and was front-loaded; do not annualize the 2025 number. |
| Balance sheet transformed | Net financial debt fell to EUR 66 million at year-end 2025 (from EUR ~480M mid-year) thanks to the EUR 295M gross disposal proceeds plus cash flow | **Matches.** Confirmed by the company's own ad-hoc disclosure. This is the most important factual change in the file. |

The pattern: the operating-margin and balance-sheet claims hold up; the growth and earnings-power claims are inflated by one-time items and a single non-recurring mega-order.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable, with a clear shift from offensive to defensive language.** In early 2024 the CEO led with order records and acquisition ambition ("building the second-largest player"). By late 2025 and early 2026 the lead-off changed to profitability and resilience ("As our main focus is on profitability, I would like to start with pointing out the high earnings level"). The vocabulary moved from "growth," "pipeline," and "battery potential" to "self-help measures," "earnings resilience," "cost savings," and "value before volume." Confidence on margins rose and became more specific; confidence on demand became more hedged and conditional ("Is it fantastic? Probably not, but it's very solid"). This is not deteriorating confidence — it is a management team that has rationally repositioned a cyclical, low-growth franchise around the lever it actually controls (cost and mix) rather than the one it doesn't (auto-OEM and furniture capital spending).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: Medium-to-High.** The company has a consistent, almost ritualized pattern of guiding conservatively and then landing at or above target. It "met or exceeded all of our targets" for 2025, beat its own free-cash-flow guide by a wide margin, and slightly exceeded the EBIT-margin corridor. The CFO is candid about sandbagging — "as you know, we are always a bit conservative... I don't want to raise the bar right now." That said, the screener's recorded beat rate against consensus is poor (1 of 7 quarters, 14%), which reflects that the lumpy, project-driven order book makes quarter-to-quarter consensus hard to beat even when full-year self-set targets are met. The honest read: trust the full-year guidance corridors; do not trust quarter-level precision.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pushed hardest, and repeatedly, on three things. First, **the battery/e-mobility business** — Baader, DZ Bank and others asked about it nearly every call, and each time management's answer softened, ending in the late-2025 admission of restructuring and impairment. The analysts were right to worry. Second, **HOMAG / furniture-market recovery** — management deflected with "not before the end of the year" for several consecutive quarters; three years in, they conceded "it's still difficult to tell when there will be a real recovery." Third, **order-intake quality and timing** — analysts probed whether large system orders carried lower margins and whether China weakness was structural; management's answers here were straight ("China is a very competitive market... it is competition," and the China book-to-bill fell to 0.4 in Q4 2025). The recurring unease analysts have that management does not fully resolve is the absence of any visible top-line growth engine now that batteries are gone.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Order intake down 29% over nine months of 2025 and another 11% in Q1 2026 — the backlog cushion is being drawn down, not rebuilt.
🔴 The headline 2025 earnings surge is a disposal gain; continuing operations lost money after impairments (EUR 135M).
🔴 EUR 100M of 2025 free cash flow was pulled-forward prepayments that reverse in 2026, with management explicitly guiding free cash flow back to EUR 0–50 million.
🔴 The battery thesis, hyped for two years, ended in restructuring and write-down — a credibility ding on management's growth-area judgment.
🔴 China structurally weakening (book-to-bill 0.4 in Q4 2025) with no clear path back.

🟢 EBIT margin before extraordinaries up 100 basis points to 5.6% in a falling-revenue year — disciplined execution.
🟢 Net debt collapsed to EUR 66 million; the balance sheet is now a genuine strength, not a constraint.
🟢 Portfolio cleaned up — two non-core sales done, five divisions cut to three, two cost programs in flight.
🟢 Dividend raised to EUR 0.80 (from 0.70) at the 2026 annual meeting — a confidence signal, even if modest.
🟢 Management is candid and consistent; it does what it says on the full-year level.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is linguistic: "growth" and "acquisition" gave way to "Sustainable Automation," "lean company," and "resizing our administrative structure." A new CFO is arriving (flagged at the 2026 annual meeting), and a new operational leader (HOMAG's former chief operating officer) was installed over the troubled BBS/Industrial Automation unit — both signs the board is prioritizing operational fix-it skills over deal-making. Management also began, late in the file, to float **defense** as a possible new end-market ("we are currently investigating... for the whole group what potentials we have to give defense a more structured approach") — an early, unquantified option, not yet a thesis. The promised **Capital Markets Day and midterm-targets/strategy update** "in the course of the year" is the one forward catalyst management has explicitly teed up, but it carries no fixed date.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE, bordering on STRENGTHENING on the capital-allocation axis specifically.** This management team has executed a textbook de-conglomeration: sold non-core at a high book gain, slashed net debt to near zero, cut two divisions and is cutting EUR 50 million of overhead, all while lifting margins in a down market. That is good stewardship of a mediocre asset.

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing: **this is a cyclical, low-return, low-growth capital-goods business whose cheapness is real but whose re-rating depends on a furniture-market and auto-capex recovery that management itself cannot date — and the load-bearing "catalyst," the environmental-technology disposal, has already happened.** The optical earnings cheapness (price-to-free-cash-flow around 4–5x) is partly an artifact of a disposal-inflated denominator; on continuing operations the multiple is far less dramatic.

**Moat:** scale-cost and intangible (engineering/installed-base/service) — Dürr is a genuine global leader in automotive paint systems and in HOMAG woodworking, with a sticky ~28% service share. But the width is **NARROW and the trend is broadly STABLE-to-eroding**: return on invested capital is only about 5% (below its cost of capital), gross margin is a thin and merely "stable" 22%, and the company competes against intense, low-cost Chinese rivals it openly respects. A leader, yes — but not one that earns excess returns.

**Secular threat:** **manageable.** The auto-paint-shop franchise is actually insulated from the electric-vehicle transition (paint shops are powertrain-agnostic and the modernization driver is energy/ESG, not drivetrain), and the battery-equipment misadventure has been written down and absorbed. There is no terminal-value killer here; the headwinds are cyclical (auto capex, furniture demand, China competition), not structural. The cheapness is therefore a fear-print on a cyclical trough, not a value trap on a melting base — but it is cheapness without a dated trigger.

Two growth drivers introduced with fanfare in 2024 were quietly buried by 2025–26. The lithium-ion battery-equipment business — talked up repeatedly in 2024 as a "double-digit million" order pipeline and "a lot of potential" — was restructured, impaired, and folded into the Automotive division by early 2026 ("It's tough to be quite fair at the moment. That's why we are restructuring," 2025-11-13). BBS Automation, acquired in 2023 to build "the second-largest player in industrial automation," took a €120 million goodwill impairment in mid-2025 and had its management replaced. The narrative that survived is narrower and more honest: a high-quality automotive-equipment franchise, a cyclically depressed but self-helped woodworking unit, and an industrial-automation division still under repair.

Management has delivered a real two-year transformation (five divisions to three, environmental business sold at a rich 227 million-euro gain, net debt to near zero, operating margin up 100 basis points to 5.6% in a falling-sales year) and has an under-promise-and-beat track record. That earns a strong value grade. But two things hold the execution conviction to the middle: first, the headline cheapness is overstated by a one-time gain and a prepayment-inflated cash-flow figure -- on normalized numbers it is ~6x enterprise-value-to-operating-EBIT, cheap but earned by a group that returns only its cost of capital; second, and decisively for the current regime, the load-bearing value-unlock catalyst has already fired, and what remains -- even with the Capital Markets Day now dated for 2026-12-09/10 -- is a cyclical auto-capex and furniture recovery bet plus a strategy-reset narrative event, not a hard resolution driver. The prevailing regime explicitly rewards hard-dated structural special-situations (distressed/deleveraging, spinoffs, forced-sellers) and penalizes exactly this kind of cyclical, macro-recovery thesis that hinges on one shared factor (industrial demand) turning. Order intake is still falling (-11% in the first quarter of 2026); the cycle has not turned. The right posture is to keep Durr on the watchlist and buy the flush -- a capitulation toward the low teens, or a disappointing Capital Markets Day that resets expectations lower -- rather than to chase it near 18 euros, still below fair-adverse value, today. Buy-the-business value conviction is high (4); catalyst-and-timing conviction is a patient hold (3, verdict B).
sop_breakdown: Base-case sum-of-the-parts ~24 euros/share on ~69.2 million shares. Automotive (through-cycle EBIT ~165 million euros at 7.5x) = ~1.24 billion euros -- the crown jewel, roughly the whole current enterprise value on its own. HOMAG/woodworking (EBIT ~80 million euros at 6x, 84% owned) = ~0.40 billion euros. Industrial Automation (normalized EBIT ~25 million euros at ~7x, still under repair) = ~0.18 billion euros. Sum ~1.82 billion euros enterprise value, less ~150 million euros net financial debt including leases = ~1.67 billion euros equity = ~24 euros. Set below the screener's 40-euro composite fair value because that figure over-credits a normalized-earnings and a one-time-gain-inflated EPS the auto cycle has not yet delivered; the EPV model's +30% margin of safety and the IV15 model's negative reading are the honest counterweights to the DCF/Graham optimism.
risk_reward: From 17.84 euros: downside to the adverse/washout case of 14 euros is about -21.5%; upside to the 24-euro base is about +34.5%; upside to the 34-euro favorable case is about +90.5%. The skew is favorable, but note the adverse *fundamental* sum-of-the-parts sits near this price band (~17 euros), so the real 'risk' is a temporary price overshoot into the low teens rather than a permanent capital loss -- which is precisely why this is a wait-for-the-flush setup, not an aggressive entry.
peer_comps_note: The peer file (Krones, GEA, ABB, Jenoptik) marks Durr as 'cheap versus peers' -- 4.2x price-to-free-cash-flow against German capital-goods peers at 12-18x, with a 50-85% margin of safety across every value method. This is treated as an INDEPENDENT relative-value lever, and it supports a genuine discount. But the peer note itself is explicit that the gap is 'largely explained by weaker quality and a structurally weak end-market': Durr's ~5% net margin and ~5% return on invested capital versus peers' 8-9% and 10%+, and an automotive-OEM paint-shop capex cycle in a real downturn. This is a quality/end-market discount, not a shared-regulatory sector beta and not idiosyncratic single-name alpha the market has simply missed -- so the full peer gap is NOT credited as edge. The normalized ~6x enterprise-value-to-operating-EBIT still leaves a real, earned discount after that haircut.
